newsitem.title: ITALY: EU should play carrot and stick with Turkey - Greece.
newsitem.headline: EU should play carrot and stick with Turkey - Greece.

text.p: Greece's deputy foreign minister said on Monday that the EU should adopt a "carrot and stick" approach to forcing Turkey to pull out of Cyprus.

"Turkey wants to move closer to Europe. Europe therefore has a strong weapon by saying (to Turkey) 'your relations will improve if you accept a just and viable solution to Cyprus'," Yannos Kranidiotis told Reuters in an interview in Rome.
"It's pressure towards Turkey but at the same time it's a carrot -- a carrot and stick approach," said Kranidiotis, who was attending a meeting of international socialist groups.
Turkey signed a key customs union with the European Union in 1996 as a prelude to possible full membership but Greece succeeded in blocking funds to Ankara due to flow from the pact.
Diplomats say Ankara is increasingly hinting that it could now block plans to expand NATO into eastern Europe unless the EU delivers on its promises of closer ties.
Cyprus has been divided since Turkey invaded in 1974 in response to a Greek Cypriot coup backed by Athens.

Tensions between Greece and Turkey have risen sharply in recent weeks following an announcement by the Greek Cypriot government that it planned to buy and install a Russian anti-aircraft missile system due for deployment in 16 months.
Turkey, which has a self-declared Turkish Cypriot republic and 30,000 troops on Cyprus, threatened to use force to halt the deployment, prompting a frantic bout of U.S. diplomacy.
Turkish Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan on Tuesday called on the Greek Cypriot administration, seen internationally as the island's only government, to announce it would scrap the deal.

Kranidiotis said he thought the time was now right for an international push to solve the Cyprus problem, but said talks on the island's accession to the European Union, due to start six months after the EU concludes this year's treaty review, should not be made conditional on a solution having been found.
German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel said on Monday that Cyprus should not join until the dispute was settled.
"The solution is not a prerequisite for the accession of Cyprus but the accession could serve as the catalyst for finding the solution," Kranidiotis said.
Greek Prime Minister Costas Simitis, in a speech to the Socialist International, accused Turkey of pursuing "a policy of aggression" in the Aegean region against international law.

Greece, which regards Turkey as a "troublemaker", has asked Turkey to engage in "a step by step approach" to solve their differences on the basis of international law. "We hope that Turkey responds positively to our initiative," Simitis said.

Kranidiotis said that included submitting their rival claims to an Aegean Sea outcrop over which the two countries almost went to war to the International Court of Justice. He said Greece would be willing to abide by its ruling.
Turkey's response had so far been negative, he said.
